notes.meaning: After the Passover celebration, the Israelites went across Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh smashing stone pillars, chopping down Asherah poles, and tearing down altars. Worshiping the true God gave them a deep desire to remove all idols from the land. They did not stop until every pagan altar was gone, and only then did they return to their hometowns.

Hezekiah organized the priests and Levites back into their regular work groups, just as King David had originally set them up. Each worker was given clear duties, such as offering sacrifices, leading prayer, or singing praises at the temple gates. God's house was meant to have orderly and steady worship every day, not just on special holidays.

The king paid for the daily morning and evening sacrifices, as well as the special offerings for Sabbaths and festivals, out of his own royal wealth. He did not place this financial burden on the people, who were recovering from difficult years. A godly leader sets a personal example of generous giving for the Lord's work.

Hezekiah ordered the people living in Jerusalem to bring in the required food portions for the priests and Levites. Giving them this support meant the temple workers did not have to leave their duties to earn a living by farming. It allowed them to focus all their energy on studying God's law and teaching it to the nation.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe the Old Testament command to give a tenth was tied to the temple priesthood and that Christians are now called to give freely and cheerfully without a set percentage.
Many evangelicals believe giving ten percent remains a biblical pattern and a helpful starting guide for supporting ministry.

notes.meaning: As soon as the king's order went out, the people responded with great generosity. They brought the first share of their harvest, including grain, new wine, olive oil, and honey or dates, along with a tithe (a tenth) of all their produce. When God renews people's hearts, they give willingly and joyfully.

The people living throughout the cities of Judah also brought a tenth of their cattle and sheep, as well as gifts pledged to the Lord. They brought in so much produce and livestock that the gifts were stacked in giant heaps in the temple courtyards.

The people began piling up these gifts in the third month, right at the start of the wheat harvest. They continued bringing in produce throughout the summer until the grape and fruit harvests ended in the seventh month. For four whole months, truckloads of fresh supplies poured into Jerusalem.

When Hezekiah and his royal officials came to the temple and saw the huge mounds of food, they praised the Lord. They thanked God for blessing the land with a rich harvest and commended the people for their generous hearts.
Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the giant heaps of food. He wanted to know why so much produce was still sitting in piles and whether the sacred workers were receiving enough to eat.

Azariah the high priest explained that the temple staff had eaten their fill ever since the people began bringing offerings. The Lord had blessed the harvest so abundantly that these massive piles were simply what was left over. God faithfully provides more than enough when His people honor Him.

Hezekiah ordered rooms in the temple complex to be prepared as secure storerooms. The workers quickly cleaned out and readied these rooms to hold the massive supply of food. Proper storage protected the gifts from spoiling, pests, and theft.

The workers faithfully moved all the tithes, firstfruits, and dedicated gifts into the storerooms. A Levite named Conaniah was put in charge of the supplies, and his brother Shimei served as his second-in-command.

Ten Levites were appointed to assist Conaniah and Shimei in managing the stored supplies. They were chosen by the authority of both King Hezekiah and Azariah, the chief leader over the house of God. Clear organization and trusted leaders kept the distribution honest.

Kore, the Levite gatekeeper of the East Gate, was placed in charge of the voluntary offerings brought to God. His duty was to receive the gifts given out of personal devotion and hand out the special portions of meat and grain set aside for the priests.

Six trusted Levites served under Kore to give out food to the priests living in the outlying priestly towns. They faithfully handed out equal shares to their fellow priests according to their work groups, young and old alike. Priests who remained in the country towns were cared for just like those serving in Jerusalem.

These local town deliveries were separate from the daily food given to priests on active duty at the temple. When priests traveled to Jerusalem to serve their assigned shift, they and their sons who were three years old or older received food directly at the temple.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars and translations read the minimum age as thirty years old rather than three, matching the traditional starting age for Levite service.

notes.meaning: The official family lists recorded the priests by their clans, and the Levites from age twenty and older were listed by their duties. King David had lowered the starting age for Levites to twenty so more men could help with temple work. These careful records ensured that only genuine workers received the holy food.

The official lists also included the wives, sons, and daughters of the priests and Levites. Because these workers had separated themselves from ordinary farming and business to serve God full time, the community made sure their whole households had food.

Special men were also appointed by name to distribute food to priests living on the pasture lands outside the towns. Every male among the priests and every Levite listed in the family records received a fair share. No family was forgotten, no matter how far away they lived.
Hezekiah carried out these reforms across the entire land of Judah, not just around his capital. In everything he did, he acted with goodness, fairness, and true loyalty before the Lord.

Hezekiah put his whole heart into every project he started for the temple and for God's law. Because his real aim was to seek God and obey Him, the Lord gave him great success in all he did. When believers seek God with a sincere heart, He honors their work.
